Figure 2 illustrates that the molecular weight distribution of the FRP-synthesized PDMAPAm is broader compared to the RAFT-synthesized versions. However, the functional performance regarding CO 2 -triggered switching remains intact, highlighting the potential of FRP for scalable and cost-effective production of CO 2 -responsive polymers. In another significant study, Huang et al. (2024) [ 75 ] developed CO 2 -responsive polymers by applying aqueous free radical copolymerization of DMAEMA and polyether-modified methacrylates with acrylamide at 45 °C, as illustrated in Figure 3 a. The resulting polymers featured tertiary amine groups and hydrophobic polyether side chains, which endowed them with gas-switchable solubility and dual responsiveness to both pH and CO 2 , making them attractive for smart hydrogel and coating applications. Likewise, Wu et al. (2023) [ 82 ] developed a CO 2 -responsive intelligent polymer sealant by using aqueous FRP of acrylamide and DMAPMA, which was cross-linked with polyethyleneimine (PEI) to improve its functionality ( Figure 3 b). The resulting polymer gel exhibited reversible swelling behavior and strong pH and CO 2 responsiveness. In the realm of nanostructured polymer systems, Yu et al. (2019) [ 83 ] revealed an innovative enzyme-assisted, photo-initiated FRP (photo-PISA) process carried out under open-air conditions. Cross-linked CO 2 -responsive polymer vesicles were synthesized through the copolymerization of HPMA and DMAEMA using a photoinitiator and an oxygen-scavenging enzyme system. The addition of the asymmetric cross-linker allyl methacrylate (AMA) provided mechanical stability, whereas DMAEMA units granted the vesicles CO 2 -switchable expansion behavior. Zhao et al. (2017) [ 48 ] investigated the new class of FRP-derived polymeric surfactants that include DEAEMA, demonstrating the ability to alter emulsification properties in oil–water systems based on the CO 2 –N 2 gas environment. This study broadened the use of FRP-based CO 2 -responsive polymers in dynamic emulsion stabilization, an important field in materials chemistry. In another significant development, Ellis et al. (2019) [ 84 ] used FRP to synthesize nitrogen-rich polyamine draw solutes for forward osmosis, allowing for the modulation of osmotic pressure and CO 2 -responsiveness through the protonation of amine groups ( Figure 4 I). Furthermore, Gupta and Lee (2017) [ 85 ] developed a pyrene-functionalized polymeric probe through FRP for the fluorescence-based detection of nerve agent mimics ( Figure 4 II). The fluorescence of the material can be reversibly activated and deactivated through CO 2 –N 2 purging, which is linked to the protonation state of amine groups affecting the photoinduced electron transfer (PET) pathway. Lastly, Fan et al. (2017) [ 86 ] developed single-chain CO 2 -responsive polymer nanoparticles (SCNPs) with free radical polymerization of copolymers, including DMAEMA ( Figure 4 III). Reversing swelling and shrinking characteristics of the nanoparticles allowed for gas-tunable control over their size and catalytic activity. Collectively, these contemporary examples illustrate that FRP is not merely a legacy method for latex production but a versatile and robust tool for constructing CO 2 -responsive polymers in various advanced formats. Despite its lack of molecular-level control compared to living radical polymerizations like RAFT or ATRP, FRP remains highly effective in producing functionally responsive materials, especially when precision in molecular weight is not a limiting factor for application. 3.2. Controlled Radical Polymerization Techniques Reversible deactivation radical polymerization (RDRP), or controlled/living radical polymerization, has transformed polymer synthesis by permitting precise regulation of molecular weight, dispersity, and polymer architecture. In contrast to conventional living polymerizations, including anionic or cationic techniques, reversible-deactivation radical polymerization (RDRP) functions under more accessible and practical conditions [ 87 ]. In FRP, the lifespan of the developing chains is very rapid (under 1 s), resulting in all polymer chains becoming “dead” after the reaction. Consequently, the polymerization is non-living, and block copolymers cannot be produced by this process [ 88 ]. Anionic polymerization, as developed by Szwarc [ 89 ], reflects a true living system in which chain transfer and termination reactions are effectively eliminated. This can only be accomplished by removing all moisture and/or oxygen, requiring high vacuum conditions and very low temperatures (approximately −80 °C) [ 90 ]. By utilizing RDRP, or living radical polymerization, various monomers can be polymerized under milder conditions commonly used in FRP, while achieving a substantial level of control over the polymer structures. Additionally, RDRP exhibits lower sensitivity to water compared to anionic polymerization, which represents a significant advantage, as numerous industrial polymerizations occur in aqueous environments, such as emulsion polymerizations for latex production. In RDRP, the minimal occurrence of irreversible termination reactions allows for chains to remain active for extended durations, ideally throughout the entire polymerization process. This enables the incorporation of additional blocks, facilitating the preparation of block copolymers [ 89 ]. Subsequent sections will demonstrate that RDRP has emerged as the preferred polymerization technique for the synthesis of CO 2 -switchable polymers characterized by complex microstructures or mesostructures, such as di- and triblock copolymers and nanostructured particles. FRP is a more straightforward and cost-effective option compared to RDRP, particularly when precise control over molecular weight distribution and complex molecular architectures is not essential. The three predominant types of reversible-deactivation radical polymerization (RDRP) are nitroxide-mediated polymerization (NMP), atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP), and reversible addition-fragmentation transfer (RAFT) polymerization. Figure 5 provides a clear summary of these mechanisms, illustrating the activation–deactivation equilibria in NMP, ATRP, and RAFT polymerization pathways [ 87 ]. The primary distinction between RDRP and FRP lies in the significant reduction of termination reactions in RDRP, achieved through the incorporation of a control agent that facilitates the reversible deactivation of propagating chains. In NMP, nitroxide is introduced to the system to deactivate propagating radicals and reduce mutual termination. ATRP employs a transition metal catalyst, whereas RAFT utilizes a chain transfer agent to decrease the occurrence of termination reactions. NMP and ATRP utilize reversible termination, whereas RAFT employs reversible chain transfer [ 91 ]. Each of these controlling mechanisms can yield a polymer characterized by low dispersity (Đ < 1.5). Numerous reviews of RDRP across various polymerization systems, including dispersed systems, have been published [ 87 , 91 , 92 , 93 ]. The application of RDRP techniques in the production of switchable materials is emerging as a significant research focus. This paper highlights the synthesis of CO 2 -switchable polymers through reversible-deactivation radical polymerization (RDRP) in the subsequent sections. 3.2.1. Atomic Transfer Radical Polymerization (ATRP) Atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP) is a prevalent method for the controlled radical polymerization of CO 2 -responsive polymers. In ATRP, there is an equilibrium between propagating radicals and dormant species [ 94 ]. The dormant species (Pn–X) are common and intermittently interact with transition metal complexes. Transition metal complexes function as activators in their lower oxidation state (Mtm/L), engaging with halide-terminated “dormant” chains to produce propagating radicals (Pn˙) and transition metal complexes in a higher oxidation state. In elevated oxidation states, transition metal complexes coordinate with halide ligands (X–Mtm+1/L) and function as deactivators. The deactivator interacts with propagating radicals to produce dormant species and the activator ( Figure 6 a). Consequently, the concentration of propagating radicals remains low in comparison to FRP, leading to a reduction in termination reactions. In certain applications, it may be necessary to remove the transition metal catalyst and ligand. This is clear for homogeneous systems; however, it can cause challenges in heterogeneous systems [ 95 ]. The versatile nature of ATRP has allowed for the development of a wide spectrum of CO 2 -switchable polymer systems. Classical copper-mediated ATRP has been utilized to synthesize diverse diblock, triblock, star-like, and surface-grafted CO 2 -responsive polymers [ 96 ]. Poly(ethylene oxide)-block-poly((N-amidino)dodecyl acrylamide) (PEO-b-PAD) was synthesized using ATRP at room temperature using CuBr/PMDETA, providing a well-defined diblock structure containing CO 2 -switchable amidine moieties. Figure 6 b illustrates the synthesis route for the preparation of PEO-b-PAD. The reaction was conducted in anhydrous methanol for 12 h, deploying pentamethyldiethylenetriamine (PMDETA) as the ligand and copper bromide (CuBr) as the catalyst [ 96 ]. Likewise, triblock copolymers like PEO-b-PS-b-PDEAEMA have been synthesized using sequential ATRP, using the tertiary amine functionality of DEAEMA for CO 2 -responsiveness. The PEO macroinitiator was prepared by conducting the ATRP of mono-methoxyl poly(ethylene oxide) in dichloromethane (CH 2 Cl 2 ) with triethylamine (TEA) at ambient temperature for 24 h, using 2-bromo-isobutyryl bromide (BiBB) as the initiator. The macroinitiator (O–Br) was used in the ATRP of styrene in bulk using copper bromide (CuBr) as the catalyst and PMDETA as the ligand ( Figure 6 c). The reaction persisted for 16 h at 110 °C to yield the OS macroinitiator for the third stage. The last phase was the ATRP of DEAEMA conducted in toluene with an OS macroinitiator, a combination of copper chlorides (CuCl and CuCl 2 ) as the catalyst, and the PMDETA ligand at 60 °C for 24 h. The PMDETA ligand was used in the production of a PDMAEMA-b-PEO-b-PDMAEMA triblock copolymer, functioning as a CO 2 -switchable nanocomposite via ATRP using a Br–PEO–Br initiator [ 97 ]. Figure 6 ( a – c ) ATRP-based synthetic approaches for constructing CO 2 -responsive polymer architectures. ( a ) Illustration of the ATRP equilibrium mechanism [ 95 ]. ( b ) Schematic synthesis pathway of the diblock copolymer PEO-b-PAD [ 96 ]. ( c ) Stepwise ATRP strategy for preparing the triblock copolymer PEO-b-PS-b-PDEAEMA [ 98 ]. Likewise, Xu et al. (2013) [ 99 ] synthesized a fluorophore–polymer conjugate, PBI–PDMAEMA, which consists of two CO 2 -switchable PDMAEMA arms and a central perylene-3,4,9,10-tetracarboxylic acid bisimide (PBI) fluorophore. This was achieved through the ATRP of DMAEMA using N,N′-bis{2-[2-[(2-bromo-2-methylpropanoyl)oxy]ethoxy]ethyl}perylene-3,4,9,10-tetracarboxylic acid bisimide initiators. Following the synthesis of the PBI–Br macroinitiator (ATRP macroinitiator), it was applied in the ATRP of DMAEMA with CuBr as the catalyst, PMDETA as the ligand, and THF as the solvent. In a recent study, Rezvani et al. (2019) [ 52 ] synthesized CO 2 -responsive polymers using the ATRP method. The process commenced with the extraction of cellulose nanocrystals (CNC) from microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) via acid hydrolysis. The CNCs were subsequently functionalized through the grafting of an ATRP initiator, α-Bromoisobutyryl bromide (BiBB), leading to the formation of CNC-Br. This step offered the essential spots for starting polymerization. The subsequent phase entailed the synthesis of copolymers through the grafting of poly(2-dimethylaminoethyl methacrylate) (PDMAEMA) and coumarin derivatives onto the CNCs. The reaction took place in tetrahydrofuran (THF), with DMAEMA and a coumarin derivative (CSA) added as monomers, while a catalyst system consisting of CuBr and PMDETA was used to initiate the polymerization ( Figure 7 ). The polymerization took place at 70 °C for 24 h, leading to the production of both free copolymers and CNC-grafted copolymers. A recent innovation is the development of organocatalyzed ATRP (O-ATRP), which removes the necessity for metal catalysts. Su et al. (2019) [ 100 ] introduced an innovative method for synthesizing both hydrophobic and hydrophilic polymers through organocatalyzed atom transfer radical polymerization (O-ATRP). This approach uses a CO 2 -switchable photocatalyst capable of reversible transitions between hydrophobic and hydrophilic states, contingent on the presence or absence of CO 2 . This catalyst’s primary characteristic is its ability to be flipped by the addition or removal of CO 2 , allowing for reuse in future polymerization processes. The photocatalyst, functionalized with tertiary amine groups, exhibits hydrophobic properties in its neutral state (CO 2 -absent) and transitions to a hydrophilic state upon protonation in the presence of CO 2 . The polymerization can be conducted in either organic or aqueous media, depending on the state of the catalyst ( Figure 8 a). The development of the CO 2 -switchable photocatalyst (compound 1) included the functionalization of diphenyldihydrophenazine with tertiary amines to facilitate CO 2 responsiveness. The catalyst demonstrates efficacy in hydrophobic polymerizations using solvents such as toluene, as well as in hydrophilic polymerizations conducted in carbonated water. The authors demonstrated that the catalyst could be effectively recycled and reused across multiple cycles, with minimal residual catalyst present in the final polymer (less than 15 ppb). The O-ATRP process was conducted using styrene (St) in toluene and hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA) in carbonated water, demonstrating effective control over polymerization and resulting in narrow molecular weight distributions. The authors investigated the recycling process, in which the catalyst was extracted from the polymerization mixture relying on CO 2 -saturated water, and following the removal of CO 2 , it was employed again in later polymerizations. Figure 8 b illustrates the synthesis of the CO 2 -switchable photocatalyst (compound 1), which highlights the recycling process of the catalyst following polymerization. This novel method offers a more sustainable approach to ATRP by enabling the reuse of the catalyst and reducing environmental impact, especially through the utilization of CO 2 as a trigger for transitioning between hydrophilic and hydrophobic states [ 100 ]. 3.2.2. Reversible Addition-Fragmentation Chain Transfer (RAFT) Polymerization RAFT polymerization is a highly versatile and widely used technique in the field of reversible deactivation radical polymerization (RDRP) methods, particularly effective for the synthesis of CO 2 -responsive polymers with exact structural control. RAFT, established in the late 1990s, uses thiocarbonylthio-based chain transfer agents (CTAs) to promote a degenerative chain transfer process involving dormant and active chains. This promotes consistent chain growth, even at higher conversions, resulting in polymers characterized by narrow molecular weight distributions and regulated architectures [ 101 ]. Figure 9 illustrates a standard kinetic scheme for RAFT polymerization. Reaction I serves as the initiation step in RAFT, analogous to FRP. During the pre-equilibrium step (reaction II), the transfer of the RAFT agent to a propagating chain results in the formation of a macroRAFT agent. Reaction IV illustrates the principal RAFT equilibrium, in which the RAFT agent is exchanged among advancing polymer chains. Propagation (reaction III) and termination (reaction V) occur in a way comparable to the FRP mechanism. RAFT accommodates a broader range of monomers compared to NMP or ATRP, making it a commonly employed technique for synthesizing well-defined (co)polymers characterized by narrow molecular weight distributions and specific end functionalities. The RAFT agent can introduce color to the product, and residual odor can be a concern, which requires the post-reaction removal of the RAFT agent from the polymer chain ends [ 101 ]. Lin et al. (2016) [ 102 ] explained a straightforward grafting method in their paper that integrates RAFT polymerization with post-polymerization modification for the synthesis of CO 2 -responsive graft copolymers. A linear copolymer of poly(N,N-dimethylacrylamide-co-pentafluorophenyl acrylate), referred to as P(DMA-co-PFPA), was synthesized using RAFT polymerization. The backbone featured reactive pentafluorophenyl ester groups, providing the subsequent grafting of amine-terminated poly(2-(diethylamino)ethyl methacrylate) (PDEAEMA), a recognized CO 2 -responsive polymer, along with optional poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) side chains. The homo-graft (PDMA-g-PDEAEMA, P4) and hetero-graft (PDMA-g-(PDEAEMA; PMMA), P5) copolymers demonstrated self-assembly into vesicular structures in aqueous media. When CO 2 was bubbled through, the vesicles expanded as a result of the protonation of tertiary amine groups on the PDEAEMA side chains. P4 demonstrated reversible swelling and shrinking when subjected to alternating purging with CO 2 and Ar, whereas P5 exhibited irreversible aggregation attributed to the presence of hydrophobic PMMA segments. In another study by Guo et al. (2022) [ 103 ], a new approach to switchable RAFT polymerization was developed to fabricate CO 2 -responsive gradient copolymers, allowing for precise control over the sequence distribution of the monomers. This method involved a proton-switchable RAFT agent that could selectively polymerize more-activated monomers (MAMs) or less-activated monomers (LAMs) by switching between their active states through an acid–base treatment. Using this technique, the researchers synthesized a triblock copolymer, PBzMA-b-P(DEAEMA-grad-NVP)-b-PNVP, where the middle block showed a gradient from hydrophobic DEAEMA to hydrophilic NVP. This gradient structure led to the formation of compartmentalized micelles with CO 2 -responsive properties. These copolymers exhibited unique morphologies compared to typical block copolymers, offering the potential for tunable self-assembly and morphological changes when exposed to CO 2 . In a similar vein, Chen et al. (2018) [ 104 ] presented a second-generation CO 2 -responsive system based on frustrated Lewis pair (FLP) chemistry, also synthesized via RAFT polymerization. In their system, two complementary block copolymers were created: one with bulky borane groups (Lewis acid) and the other with phosphine groups (Lewis base). When CO 2 was bubbled through the mixture, these components formed cross-linked micelles via dative bonding, with CO 2 acting as a bridge between the two blocks. These FLP-based micelles demonstrated an impressively fast CO 2 -responsiveness (less than 20 s), as well as thermal reversibility and recyclability. Moreover, the micelles were used as nanocatalysts in the conversion of C1 feedstocks, opening up new possibilities in sustainable chemistry. The process of self-assembly and catalysis with these FLP-based micelles is depicted in Figure 10 . Amphiphilic block copolymers composed of poly(methacrylic acid) (PMAA) and poly(2-dimethylaminoethyl methacrylate) (PDMAEMA) serve as emulsifiers in the RAFT-mediated emulsion polymerization of PMMA latex particles. Through the modification of PDMAEMA block length and pH during polymerization, latex particles with surfaces enriched in either PDMAEMA or PMAA were synthesized in another study. The particles demonstrated bidirectional responsiveness to CO 2 ; those with PDMAEMA surfaces precipitated at elevated pH levels and redispersed on CO 2 exposure, but PMAA-surfaced particles exhibited the inverse behavior. This dual responsiveness helped reversible transitions between dispersion and precipitation, presenting a novel approach for intelligent colloidal systems [ 60 ]. Table 1 presents a summary of different CO 2 -responsive polymers synthesized through RAFT polymerization, a controlled and living radical polymerization method [ 105 ]. These polymers often include functional groups like tertiary amines, amidines, or guanidines that interact with CO 2 via reversible chemical processes. RAFT allows for the accurate regulation of molecular weight, block composition, and end-group functionality, rendering it particularly effective for the synthesis of block copolymers, micelles, and nanostructures that experience CO 2 -induced phase transitions or self-assembly [ 103 ]. 3.2.3. Nitroxide-Mediated Polymerization (NMP) Nitroxide-mediated polymerization (NMP) represents one of the earliest and strongest-established techniques among controlled radical polymerization (CRP) methods. NMP relies on a stable nitroxide radical, commonly TEMPO or analogous compounds, to reversibly deactivate growing polymer chains, which promotes polymerization with minimal termination. NMP offers a significant advantage over traditional free radical polymerization (FRP) by enabling precise control over molecular weight and producing narrow molecular weight distributions [ 115 ]. In the 1980s, Solomon et al. identified that radicals produced during free radical polymerization can be captured by nitroxides, which leads to the formation of controlled and living low molecular weight polymers [ 116 ]. In 1993, Georges and colleagues [ 117 ] applied 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidinyl-N-oxyl (TEMPO) as a nitroxide in the living radical polymerization of styrene, leading to polystyrene with a narrow molecular weight distribution. This research established the basis for nitroxide-mediated polymerization. In NMP, an alkoxyamine encounters homolytic decomposition, resulting in the formation of nitroxide and initiator radicals [ 118 ]. Nitroxides are stable radicals that typically do not self-terminate, but they can react with growing radicals to deactivate them. The activation of a nitroxide-terminated polymer chain occurs roughly every 10 2 to 10 3 s, while deactivation happens quickly, around ∼10 −3 s. During the brief period between activation and deactivation, a small number of monomers (usually 1 to 5) are added to the growing chains, resulting in polymers with a narrow molecular weight distribution (MWD) [ 90 ]. While nitroxides do not participate in irreversible termination reactions, propagating radicals may still terminate through mutual interactions. As conversion progresses, some irreversible termination occurs, increasing the ratio of nitroxide radicals to propagating radicals. Alkoxyamines typically require activation at elevated temperatures (>90 °C). Therefore, using nitroxide-mediated polymerization (NMP) to synthesize CO 2 -switchable polymers in a CO 2 atmosphere is not practical, as CO 2 -switchable monomers would be protonated in that environment. High pressure would be needed to ensure sufficient CO 2 dissolution. Alternatively, CO 2 -switchable groups can be protonated with strong acids, such as HCl, but this may cause the polymers to lose their CO 2 -switchable properties unless the acid is neutralized with a base and the residual salts are washed away. Well-defined CO 2 -switchable polymers can be synthesized via NMP in a nitrogen atmosphere. For example, Zhou et al.(2009) [ 119 ] synthesized poly(p-chloromethylstyrene)-co-polystyrene (PCMS-co-PS) with low molar dispersity using NMP. They then modified this polymer to poly(p-azidomethylstyrene)-co-polystyrene (PAMS-co-PS) and introduced amidine groups through Staudinger ligation. This polymer demonstrated a neutral–charged–neutral transition in DMF with 0.5% H 2 O by alternately introducing CO 2 and N 2 , which was confirmed by noticeable changes in the polymer’s conductivity ( Figure 11 ). Recently, Glasing et al. (2017) [ 120 ] used a grafting methodology to alter cellulose nanocrystals (CNC) with CO 2 -responsive polymers using nitroxide-mediated polymerization (NMP). This method involved the functionalization of the CNC surface with SG1-capped poly(2-dimethylaminoethyl methacrylate) (PDEAEMA) and poly(N-3-(dimethylamino)propyl methacrylamide) (PDMAPMAm) macroalkoxyamines. The synthesis of these CO 2 -responsive polymers was conducted in bulk via NMP, facilitating precise control over molecular weight, dispersity, and end-group fidelity. The grafting method enabled a comprehensive analysis of the preformed functional polymers before their attachment to the CNC surface, the initial step in the synthesis of PDEAEMA and PDMAPMAm, using NHS-BlocBuilder and 10 mol% styrene as a co-monomer in bulk at a temperature of 80 °C. This step indicates the polymerization of the monomers PDEAEMA and PDMAPMAm using the SG1-capped nitroxide as a radical initiator, facilitating well-controlled polymerization. Subsequently, CNC was modified with Glycidyl methacrylate (GMA), which is essential for introducing reactive sites on the CNC surface, thereby facilitating the subsequent grafting of CO 2 -responsive polymers. The modification of the CNC surface with GMA is essential for the subsequent Surface-Initiated NMP (SI-NMP) process, in which the functionalized CNC acts as a macro-initiator for the growth of CO 2 -responsive polymer chains. The CO 2 -responsive graft copolymers demonstrated reversible alterations in surface properties when exposed to CO 2 , shifting between hydrophobic and hydrophilic states. The ability to switch behavior presents opportunities for applications in nanocomposites, drug delivery systems, and wastewater treatment, where the modulation of surface properties is advantageous [ 120 ]. In a further investigation, surface-initiated nitroxide-mediated polymerization (SI-NMP) was chosen to graft CO 2 -responsive polymers onto cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs). CNCs were initially functionalized using an SG1-based alkoxyamine (CNC-BB), which acted as a macroinitiator. The functionalized CNCs underwent polymerization with 2-dimethylaminoethyl methacrylate (DMAEMA), diethylaminoethyl methacrylate (DEAEMA), and 3-(dimethylamino)propyl methacrylamide (PDMAPMAm) in a nitrogen atmosphere at 85 °C, utilizing styrene as a co-monomer to enhance polymerization control. The grafted CO 2 -responsive polymers demonstrated reversible transitions between hydrophilic and hydrophobic states when exposed to CO 2 . The full process starts with the synthesis of CNC–macroalkoxyamine (CNC–BB) and the subsequent grafting polymerization of DMAEMA, DEAEMA, and PDMAPMAm onto the CNC surface via SI-NMP. This method allows for the precise control of polymer grafting, enabling the creation of CO 2 -responsive CNC-based materials [ 53 ]. Table 2 provides a comparative analysis of the primary polymerization methods used for the synthesis of CO 2 -responsive polymers. Conventional free radical polymerization (FRP) continues to be popular because of its straightforward nature and affordability, particularly for the production of homopolymers or random copolymers. Nonetheless, it provides restricted control over molecular architecture. In contrast, controlled radical polymerization techniques like ATRP, RAFT, and NMP offer precise control over molecular weight, composition, and block architecture, which are essential for customizing CO 2 -responsiveness in self-assembled systems and stimuli-responsive applications. For example, ATRP facilitates the synthesis of precisely defined block copolymers with functional chain ends, whereas RAFT provides remarkable versatility for a wide array of monomers and reaction conditions. Consequently, these controlled methods are more appropriate when reproducibility, responsiveness, and functional complexity are essential in different applications. The comparative table effectively emphasizes their advantages and disadvantages [ 121 , 122 ].
title: CO<sub>2</sub>-Responsive Vinyl Polymers: From Synthesis to Application.

text: Step 1: Synthesis of Phanorod-ICG 1-1. Resuspend the phanorods (3.3 μM Au) in PBS buffer (pH 7.5). Add 5 mM ICG-NH 2 along with 5 mM NHS and 10 mM EDC into the buffer solution. Add 10 mM EDC every 30 min twice and stir overnight. Critical Step EDC is rapidly hydrolyzed in water. Adding EDC in this stepwise manner can improve the loading efficiency of ICG onto the phanorods. 1-2. Purify the phanorod-ICG by dialysis for 48 h in the dark. Collect the phanorod-ICG sample by centrifugation (2000 rcf × 15 min). Critical Step Avoid excessive speed or duration of centrifugation to prevent aggregation. If needed, the particles may be concentrated by ultrafiltration.
title: Real-Time <i>in Vivo</i> Bacterial Imaging by Computed Tomography and Fluorescence Using Phage-Gold Nanorod Bioconjugates as Contrast Agents.

text: 1 Introduction The increasing global demand for energy, coupled with the depletion of conventional energy sources, is putting immense pressure on the world's energy supply. [ 1 ] Additionally, the extraction and utilization of conventional energy sources, such as petroleum refining and thermal power, contribute substantial pollutants and greenhouse gas emissions, posing a serious threat to the environment. Consequently, the transition to renewable energy sources is becoming essential to reduce dependence on traditional energy resources. Among these renewable energy sources, solar energy and green electrical energy are notable for their abundant reserves and convenience, respectively. To sustainably harness these energy resources, green and efficient conversion technologies are essential. [ 2 , 3 ] Given catalysis's ability to efficiently produce chemicals and materials in an atomically economical way, electrocatalysis and photocatalysis have gained increasing prominence as potential energy conversion technologies in addressing societal needs and advancing sustainable development. [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] Electrocatalysis and photocatalysis are promising technologies that convert renewable electrical and solar energy into chemical energy, respectively, culminating in redox reactions facilitated by catalysts. [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] Although the potential of photocatalysis and electrocatalysis for energy conversion has been acknowledged, their practical application encounters challenges. A significant challenge is the low efficiency of catalysts in energy conversion. Generally, the energy conversion efficiency of these electrocatalysis and photocatalysis depends on the activity and selectivity of the catalysts. More exactly, the activity and selectivity of catalysts are primarily controlled by the active center and coordination environment. While the active center plays a dominant role, the coordination environment is essential as well, because it can stabilize the catalyst and regulate the electronic structure of the active center. [ 15 ] Therefore, it is necessary to enhance the catalytic effect of catalysts by designing their coordination environment. Nature provides insightful guidelines for catalyst design. Enzymes, as nature's catalysts, exhibit extremely high catalytic activity and selectivity in specific reactions. The specificity of enzymes stems not only from the enzyme's active site but also from the binding motifs and spatial configuration of its active site. According to the transition state theory, the high specificity and catalytic activity of enzymes are closely linked to the coordination environment consisting of a confined space around its active site, often termed the second coordination sphere. [ 16 ] This confined spatial structure lowers the energy barrier from the reactant to the transition state, facilitating the formation of products. [ 17 ] Inspired by enzymes, scientists started designing artificial catalysts featuring confined space to achieve higher catalytic activity. The significant development of nanomaterials has spurred a wealth of research on nanoconfined catalysts. Nanoconfined catalysts refer to catalysts that enable reactions to occur within spaces where at least one dimension is confined to the nanoscale range, typically less than 100 nm. They often feature a well‐defined hierarchical structure consisting of a substrate and active centers. [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] The substrate is the primary structure that creates the nanoconfined space and serves as the molecular container for the nanoconfined catalytic reaction. The active centers are the secondary structure anchored in the nanoconfined space and are either part of the substrate or introduced into the nanoconfined space during post‐processing. This structure regulates both the structural and electronic properties of the active center at the nanometer or even atomic scale through a coordination environment, enabling the electronic state of the active center to match the energy level of the substrate. [ 15 ] Modifying the electronic state of the active center adjusts the adsorption energy of catalytic intermediates and improves the catalytic reaction kinetics, thereby tuning the catalytic activity and selectivity. [ 21 ] Due to this ingenious nanoconfined structure, nanoconfined electrocatalysis, and photocatalysis have advanced significantly in renewable energy conversion. A timely summary of recent research progress in these areas can therefore provide valuable guidance for future developments in the field. Although several reviews have covered nanoconfinement, they generally focus on specific types of nanoconfined spaces, [ 15 , 22 , 23 ] specific materials, [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] or certain aspects of nanoconfined reactions. [ 27 , 28 , 29 ] To the best of our knowledge, there is still a lack of comprehensive examination of the thermodynamics and kinetics of nanoconfined reactions, the construction methods and properties of primary and secondary structures, and the unique effects of nanoconfined catalysts on electrocatalysis and photocatalysis. In this review, we aim to provide a systematic perspective on nanoconfined catalysts and their applications in electrocatalytic and photocatalytic energy conversion. First, we summarize the fundamentals and properties of reactions occurring in nanoconfined catalysts, including chemical equilibrium, Gibbs free energy, thermodynamic properties of fluids, diffusion, adsorption, activation, and reaction. Then, we elaborate on nanoconfined catalysts in terms of primary structure and secondary structure. Primary structures are divided mainly into general and special nanoconfined spaces based on the geometric structure of nanoconfined spaces. Secondary structures are classified as single atoms, molecules, and nanoparticles. Subsequently, we introduce the applications of nanoconfined catalysts in electrocatalytic and photocatalytic energy conversion, including hydrogen and oxygen evolution, carbon dioxide conversion, hydrogen peroxide production, and nitrogen fixation. Finally, we explore the prospects and challenges of using nanoconfined catalysts to innovate sustainable energy conversion. It is important to note that the nanoconfinement emphasized in this paper refers to the role of nano space in spatially confining reactions, which should be distinguished from quantum confinement associated with electronic states induced by size effects. 2 Fundamentals and Properties Nanoconfined catalysis involves three main steps: the encapsulation of reactants, subsequent chemical reactions, and product extraction. The interactions between the nanoconfinement and reactants, transition states, products, or catalysts fundamentally alter the energy profile and pathways of the reactions. To a certain extent, the design of nanoconfinement can effectively enhance reaction rate, selectivity, and stability. [ 30 ] Given that both photocatalysis and electrocatalysis are essentially charge‐carrier‐driven redox reactions, the various effects of nanoconfinement on conventional catalysis may also prove effective in photocatalysis and electrocatalysis. This section primarily delves into the fundamental principles and properties associated with nanoconfined catalysis. We analyze nanoconfined catalysis considering thermodynamics and kinetics, encompassing chemical equilibrium, Gibbs free energy, thermodynamic properties of fluids, diffusion, adsorption, activation, and reaction ( Figure 1 ). Figure 1 Illustration of some thermodynamic aspects (including chemical equilibrium, Gibbs free energy, and fluid thermodynamic properties) and kinetic processes (including diffusion, adsorption, activation, and reaction) involved in nanoconfined catalytic reactions. 2.1 Thermodynamics 2.1.1 Chemical Equilibrium From a thermodynamic perspective, to accelerate reaction rates and favorably shift reaction equilibria, one can strategically design reaction sites in alignment with Le Chatelier's principle to enhance the concentration of reactants or facilitate the extraction of products ( Figure 2 ). [ 31 , 32 ] For example, the enrichment of reactants can be easily achieved by structuring confined spaces with inner surfaces possessing charges opposite to those of the reactants. Guest reactants within these confined spaces often exhibit increased reactivity due to geometric confinements on pre‐organized molecules and a predilection for host‐guest interactions, or an elevation in effective concentration. [ 33 ] Consequently, reactions within confined spaces, such as droplets, manifest thermodynamic shifts favoring product formation compared to reactions in bulk solutions. This shift (δ) is associated with a dimensionless number (Equation 1 ): (1) δ = D K − 1 R 2 where D represents the diffusion coefficient, R is the droplet radius, and K −1 is the reverse reaction rate constant. Obviously, the efficiency of reactions would be heightened within small droplets. [ 27 , 34 ] Figure 2 Chemical equilibria comparison between (a) common and (b) nanoconfined reactions. The entropy also influences the chemical equilibrium in nanoconfined systems. [ 35 ] In contrast to the behavior observed in larger systems governed by classical thermodynamics, the impact of entropy on chemical equilibrium within nanoconfined systems leads to a modification of the equilibrium constant. This is evident in the greater values of both the equilibrium constant and the degree of reaction compared to their corresponding thermodynamic limit values. This phenomenon depends not only on the size of systems but also on factors such as stoichiometric coefficients of reactants, reaction energies, reaction mechanisms, and variations in stoichiometry. Consequently, the equilibrium constant is inapplicable to the reaction in a nanoconfined space, given its reliance on multiple factors. Additionally, in weakly exothermic reactions, systems with nanoconfinement yield more stable products. [ 36 ] Polak et al. termed this phenomenon the “nanoconfinement entropic effect”, emphasizing that chemical equilibria involving a limited number of molecules in a nanoconfined space may significantly deviate from macroscopic thermodynamic limits due to reduced entropy of mixing. [ 35 , 36 ] When reactions take place with a small number of molecules within the nanoconfined space, the equilibrium position can shift toward the products by reducing the number of microstates associated with reactant‐product mixing. [ 37 ] Essentially, the entropy of mixing is diminished in such a nanoconfined space and may even vanish in reactions involving two reactant molecules. [ 35 ] 2.1.2 Gibbs Free Energy Nanoconfined systems exhibit distinct thermodynamic behaviors compared to conventional catalytic systems, primarily due to their unique effects on enthalpy (Δ H ) and entropy (Δ S ). In nanoconfined environments, the reduction in entropy arises from a decrease in molecular disorder. [ 38 ] Van der Waals dispersion forces, coupled with the physical constraints imposed by nanoconfined spaces, restrict molecular degrees of freedom, including rotational and translational motions. These restrictions enhance intermolecular cohesion, significantly decreasing the entropy of the system, particularly when the pore size aligns closely with the dimensions of reactants or intermediates. [ 39 ] Additionally, in liquid‐phase reactions, the reorganization of solvent molecules around reactants and intermediates within nanoconfined spaces further reduces entropy by creating a more ordered solvent environment. Generally, the entropy loss resulting from the reduced molecular disorder is often accompanied by a significant decrease in enthalpy, reflecting the compensatory relationship between these two thermodynamic parameters. [ 40 ] According to the thermodynamic relationship Δ G = Δ H − T Δ S , a reduction in entropy and an increase in enthalpy lead to a rise in Gibbs free energy, which adversely affects reaction feasibility. However, nanoconfinement can mediate the enthalpy‐entropy compensation, altering the Gibbs free energy of reacting molecules and subsequently determining the turnover rate as described by transition state theory. [ 41 ] Within nanoconfined spaces, the pronounced decrease in enthalpy typically outweighs the negative impact of entropy reduction, particularly at relatively low temperatures, resulting in a net reduction in Δ G . This enthalpy reduction is closely associated with the stabilization of surface intermediates in confined environments. Enhanced van der Waals forces and other weak interactions, such as hydrogen bonding and π–π interactions, between molecules and pore walls significantly lower the enthalpy of intermediates and transition states, thereby reducing the overall energy of the system. [ 41 ] Concurrently, electronic interactions between active sites and reactants, such as coordination effects at metal sites or interactions with surface acid‐base sites, further stabilize key intermediates, contributing to enthalpy reduction. Consequently, despite the entropy reduction, the substantial enthalpy decrease in nanoconfined spaces reduces Gibbs free energy, ultimately accelerating reaction rates. For example, in dimethyl ether carbonylation, high specificity is observed within the small voids of FER and MOR zeolite structures, while the reaction rates are negligible in larger voids, such as those in MFI and FAU zeolites. [ 42 ] The stronger van der Waals stabilization provided by smaller voids reduces ion‐pair enthalpies, and although entropies are also decreased, the enthalpic contributions prevail. As a result, activation‐free energies for carbonylation are significantly lower in these nanoconfined spaces, highlighting the critical role of enthalpy‐entropy trade‐offs in driving reactions under confinement. Nanoconfinement can thermodynamically stabilize intermediates by modulating the Gibbs free energy of the transition state. [ 43 , 44 , 45 , 46 , 47 ] For instance, Brønsted acid sites in zeolites, located within molecular‐sized channels, stabilize adsorbed species such as monomers and transition states more effectively than the surfaces of polyoxometalate clusters, primarily through van der Waals interactions. These van der Waals forces influence the activation barrier by selectively stabilizing the transition state and its precursor reactants. Carr et al. demonstrated that during the dehydration of methanol to produce dimethyl ether, the transition state involves two methanol molecules at the active site, whereas the monomeric intermediate involves only one methanol molecule, with the other remaining in the gas phase. [ 45 ] Consequently, the nanoconfinement effect in zeolites preferentially stabilizes the transition state via van der Waals forces, making the direct pathway for dimethyl ether formation more favorable on zeolites compared to polyoxometalate clusters. Notably, nanoconfined spaces stabilize reaction intermediates through a combination of complementary mechanisms, including thermodynamic modulation, enhanced van der Waals forces, electronic effect modulation, restricted molecular motion, altered solvation effects, and synergistic multiphase interactions. First, nanoconfined spaces alter the thermodynamic equilibrium of reactions, stabilizing specific intermediates or transition states by lowering their free energy and steering the reaction pathway toward the desired products. Second, the unique structural properties of these spaces, characterized by pores or cavities on the molecular scale, intensify van der Waals interactions between intermediates and surrounding surfaces. [ 44 ] These enhanced intermolecular attractions effectively reduce the free energy of intermediates, thereby stabilizing their presence. Third, surface active sites within nanoconfined spaces form stronger bonds with intermediates through electronic interactions, such as ligand coordination or charge transfer, lowering activation energy and prolonging intermediate lifetimes. Fourth, physical constraints within nanoconfined spaces limit the movement of intermediates, reducing opportunities for decomposition or side reactions. For instance, channels or pores with dimensions comparable to those of the intermediates restrict diffusion and excessive rotation, further enhancing stability. Fifth, in solution‐phase reactions, nanoconfined spaces alter solvation conditions, including the dielectric constant of nanoconfined water, ionic hydration, and the arrangement of solvent molecules around intermediates, thereby lowering activation barriers and enhancing intermediate stability. [ 30 ] Finally, the inner surfaces of nanoconfined spaces simultaneously exhibit multiple interactions, such as hydrogen bonding, π–π interactions, and electrostatic forces, that synergistically stabilize intermediates. [ 4 ] By integrating these mechanisms, nanoconfined spaces effectively lower the energy levels of intermediates during catalytic reactions, resulting in improved reaction efficiency and selectivity ( Figure 3 ). [ 38 ] Figure 3 A schematic diagram illustrating the energy profile of a hypothetical reaction under both general and confinement conditions. Reproduced with permission. [ 38 ] Copyright 2021, Wiley‐VCH. 2.1.3 Thermodynamic Properties of Fluids In addition to influencing the chemical equilibrium and Gibbs free energy of reactions, nanoconfinement can thermodynamically induce alterations in fluid properties. Within nanoconfined spaces, fluids manifest distinct thermodynamic properties compared to the bulk phase, primarily attributable to the size of the systems [ 48 ] and the pronounced fluid‐wall interactions resulting from the enclosure. [ 49 , 50 ] In the proximity of the wall, the fluid exhibits laminar density, [ 51 , 52 , 53 , 54 ] a phenomenon arising from entropic and energetic effects due to the restricted motion of molecules and their interactions with the solid wall. [ 55 , 56 , 57 , 58 ] These entropic and energetic effects, combined with heightened fluctuations in thermodynamic properties, result in nanoconfined fluids displaying significantly different physical behavior, including alterations in phase transitions and transport properties. [ 59 , 60 , 61 , 62 , 63 ] For instance, the phase behavior of water confined within carbon nanotubes is modified and closely correlates with the diameter of the tubular confined space. [ 64 , 65 , 66 , 67 , 68 ] Similar confinement‐induced changes in phase behavior are observed in planar laminations of slit pores, such as parallel graphene sheets. [ 69 , 70 , 71 , 72 ] Moreover, when the nanoconfined space is restricted to a few nanometers or even less than a nanometer, the hydrogen‐bonding network of water undergoes substantial structural changes, exhibiting unique structural, thermodynamic, and kinetic properties. [ 73 ] 2.2 Dynamics In heterogeneous catalysis, reactions on the solid catalyst surface encompass the elementary reaction steps: diffusion of reactants to the surface, adsorption of reactants, activation of reactants, surface reactions, desorption, and diffusion of product(s) away from the surface. [ 74 ] Each of these fundamental steps may impact the overall reaction kinetics. In general, the nanoconfined environment can profoundly modify chemical reactions, influenced by alterations in adsorption, geometrical constraints, surface potentials, and other factors. For instance, favorable interactions between incoming nanoparticles and the functional groups of the confining framework contribute to the self‐assembly of nanoparticles in the nanoconfined space. [ 75 ] Moreover, variations in electronic structure and spatial confinement result in more robust strains and deformations. [ 23 ] Consequently, catalysis under confinement is anticipated to furnish a versatile platform for regulating the kinetics of catalytic reactions. 2.2.1 Diffusion Diffusion stands as a ubiquitous phenomenon in chemical reactions, representing a spontaneous process adept at leveraging the chemical potential gradient to minimize the Gibbs free energy. [ 76 , 77 , 78 ] Diffusion is typically delineated by Fickian diffusivity and self‐diffusivity. Fickian diffusivity pertains to mass transfer induced by the chemical potential gradient, while self‐diffusivity characterizes the thermal motion of the system in equilibrium, where the chemical potential gradient is null. [ 79 ] A profound comprehension of diffusive behavior in catalytic reactions is imperative, given that the accessibility of molecules, along with their permeation and partitioning dynamics, not only constrains the overall rate of the chemical reaction but also profoundly influences product selectivity. Thiele's “reaction‐diffusion” theory provides a framework for categorizing catalytic reactions into diffusion‐limited and reaction‐limited types. [ 80 ] In the context of diffusion‐limited catalytic reactions, the diffusion rate proves to be slower than the turnover rate of a specific active site. Consequently, the catalytic site remains unsaturated with reactants, implying that some of the catalytic sites remain unutilized. To unlock the full potential of the catalyst, it becomes imperative for the diffusion rate of the reactants to surpass the catalytic turnover rate, ensuring the complete utilization of catalytic sites. Within nanoconfined spaces, fluid diffusion manifests distinct properties compared to its macroscopic counterpart. [ 81 , 82 ] Notably, the structural arrangement among fluid molecules differs from that observed in the bulk phase. Bernardina et al. delved into the alterations in the hydrogen bonding network of water during its transport within CNTs. [ 83 ] In CNTs possessing a diameter of 0.8 nm, water molecules exhibit a coordination number equal to or less than 2, forming a 1D chain structure. In CNTs with a diameter of 1.4 nm, hydroxyl groups, dangling at the edges of the water molecule layer, are directed toward the tube wall. Moreover, the fluid's resistance to flow deviates from macroscopic predictions. Hinds et al. demonstrated a substantial acceleration in the flow of water molecules within the hydrophobic cavities of CNTs, registering 3–4 orders of magnitude faster than the macroscopic flow rate. [ 84 ] In such scenarios, fluid flow induces a velocity slip over the wall, attributed to the significant distinctions between wall and fluid properties. Remarkably, water molecules exhibit sliding behavior on hydrophobic graphene surfaces, covering distances up to 65 nm, with corresponding slip rates surpassing 24 m s −1 . [ 85 ] The highly diverse diffusion behaviors observed in nanoconfined spaces are primarily influenced by the geometric structures of guest molecules and nanoconfined spaces, as well as the interactions among guest molecules and between guest molecules and the nanoconfined space ( Figure 4 ). [ 86 ] First, distinct geometries of guest molecules give rise to different molecular diffusion kinetics. For instance, there is a specific size of monatomic guest molecule maximizing their diffusion rate in zeolites Y and A. [ 87 ] Also, the diffusion rate of branched alkanes in silicalite is notably slower compared to that of n‐alkanes. [ 88 , 89 ] Figure 4 Factors affecting molecular diffusion in nanoconfined spaces. Second, the geometry of the nanoconfined space has a significant impact on molecular diffusion. [ 90 ] For instance, a variation in the pore aperture of metal‐organic frameworks (MOFs) results in changes in the diffusion rates of propane and propylene. [ 91 ] Water molecules traverse carbon nanotubes with diameters comparable to their sizes in a unique manner. In this mode, water molecules do not collide with the pore walls but diffuse in a 1D ordered chain structure held in place by hydrogen bonding. [ 92 ] Investigating methane and helium molecules, Jakobtorweihen et al. discovered that their self‐diffusivity reaches a maximum at specific values of carbon nanotube size. [ 93 ] Third, interactions among guest molecules influence diffusion behavior through the mean free path. The interaction among guest molecules primarily alters the mean free path, representing the average distance traveled by a moving molecule before changing its direction or energy. In instances where the density of diffusing molecules is low and the mean free path exceeds the pore size of the nanoconfined space due to molecular collisions, the diffusion rate is 2–3 orders of magnitude lower than that in the bulk phase. [ 94 ] This circumstance can result in significant transport resistance in catalytic reactions. When the density of diffusing molecules is high, increased collisions between guest molecules and reduced free pore volume contribute to a decrease in the diffusion coefficient. Finally, interactions between guest molecules and nanoconfined spaces influence diffusion behavior through mean free path and adsorption or desorption events. On the one hand, collisions between guest molecules and nanoconfined spaces change the mean free path, thus influencing diffusion behavior. On the other hand, the diffusion behavior is also affected by the incidence of adsorption or desorption events. When these interactions do not impede molecular diffusion, the diffusion is termed non‐activated. Conversely, when adsorption and desorption events restrict molecular diffusion, it is referred to as activated diffusion. The diffusion coefficient ( D ) for activated diffusion follows an Arrhenius‐type dependence (Equation 2 ): (2) D = D 0 e x p − E A R T where E A represents the diffusion activation energy, R is the gas constant, T is the absolute temperature, and D 0 is the maximum diffusion coefficient at infinite temperature. This E A is influenced by factors such as hydrogen bonding, desorption, and adsorption processes, and the curvature of the diffusion space. [ 95 ] It is evident that diffusion in the nanoconfined space is activated diffusion and possesses a markedly different diffusion coefficient compared to the bulk state, primarily due to the unique hydrogen bonding network, adsorption and desorption behaviors, and pore curvature in the nanoconfined space altering the E A . Furthermore, the interaction between the guest molecule and the nanoconfined space is related to several parameters. 1) Guest molecule polarity: The diffusion of polar molecules within the nanoconfined space is slower compared to nonpolar molecules due to strong interactions with the host matrix. [ 96 , 97 ] 2) Guest molecule concentration: In the layered nanoconfined structure of hydrotalcite, the kinetics of water diffusion depend on water concentration. At low concentrations, the strong interaction of water molecules with hydrotalcite significantly limits kinetics. As the concentration increases, the interaction decreases, and the water diffusion constant approaches the bulk value. [ 98 ] 3) Pore size and curvature in nanoconfined space: Milischuk and Ladanyi, through molecular simulations, found that the diffusion coefficient of water in silica pores increases with pore size. [ 99 ] Both translational and rotational motions of water are significantly affected by the distance from the wall surface. Translational mobility slows notably in the water layer near the wall surface of silica. It is essential to note that the curvature of the silica pores has a relatively minor effect on the diffusion rate of water. In contrast, in anticlastic micelles with spherical nanoconfined spaces, water mobility is markedly affected by the wall curvature. [ 100 , 101 ] 4) Diffusion activation energy barrier: The small size of the nanoconfined space enhances host‐guest interactions, resulting in a high activation energy barrier for diffusion. For instance, ligand‐unsaturated metal sites and Brønsted acid sites in MOFs create high activation energy barriers, hindering mass transfer via site‐hopping. [ 102 , 103 , 104 ] The reactions of converting renewable energy into chemicals often involve proton transfer, including hydrogen evolution, oxygen reduction, carbon dioxide reaction, and nitrogen reduction. Two primary proton transport mechanisms are generally considered: the vehicle and Grotthuss mechanisms ( Figure 5 ). [ 105 ] The vehicle mechanism involves the migration of protons through the medium along with the proton solvent. On the other hand, the Grotthuss mechanism, also known as proton hopping, entails the diffusion of protons through a network of hydrogen bonds accompanied by the formation and cleavage of covalent bonds. [ 106 ] The Grotthuss mechanism is thought to have two modes of proton transport: the Eigen to Zundel to Eigen (E‐Z‐E) and Zundel to Zundel (Z‐Z) modes (Figure 5c,d ). [ 107 , 108 ] The E‐Z‐E mode is considered the most plausible mechanism for proton diffusion in bulk water. Figure 5 Proton transport mechanisms. a) Vehicle mechanism and b) Grotthuss mechanism of proton transport. c) E‐Z‐E mode and d) Z‐Z mode of the Grotthuss mechanism. Nanoconfinement can shift the diffusion mode of protons. In hydrophobic nanochannels where water molecules are confined, protons are anticipated to diffuse through the Z‐Z mode. [ 109 ] This mode enables more efficient jumping between neighboring sites due to less redirection and interconversion energy. [ 110 , 111 ] Moreover, the influence of nanoconfinement on proton hopping diffusion may become more pronounced in low‐dimensional nanopores. For instance, the proton diffusion process can be nearly barrier‐free in a 2D confined space. [ 71 , 112 , 113 ] Furthermore, in hydrophobic nanochannels with smaller pore sizes, the number of neighboring water molecules in the nanoconfined space decreases, and the mobility of the nanoconfined water molecules is expected to increase. [ 114 ] An illustrative instance is the notable mobility of water molecules observed in hydrophobic carbon nanotube channels. [ 92 , 111 ] This enhanced mobility can be elucidated through two perspectives. [ 115 ] First, from a thermodynamic standpoint, when the diameter of carbon nanotubes approximates or slightly exceeds the motion radius of water molecules, these molecules disengage from the bulk fluid, spontaneously infiltrate the carbon nanotubes, and eventually assemble into a 1D single chain—a process driven by an increase in entropy. [ 92 ] Second, considering kinetics, the inner surface of carbon nanotubes lacks polarity, resulting in minimal friction between water molecules and the tube wall. [ 116 ] Consequently, water molecules can swiftly traverse through carbon nanotubes. Absolutely, the impact of ion diffusion on energy conversion reactions needs to be meticulously considered in the context of charge transport, particularly in electrocatalysis. Efficient electrochemical conversion necessitates high diffusion rates for both electrons and electrolyte ions to ensure their arrival at the active site. Yet, the reciprocal effect, how charge transport influences ion diffusion, is frequently disregarded. In electrocatalysis, substantial electron migration induces shifts in local charge concentrations, prompting compromises in the diffusion rates of ions and electrons to maintain electroneutrality. [ 117 , 118 , 119 ] Specifically, the rapid movement of electrons or ions creates an uncompensated electric field, retarding carriers or ions of the same charge while accelerating those of the opposite charge, thereby contributing to electroneutrality preservation. [ 118 ] Besides, the ion diffusion constant is typically orders of magnitude lower than the electron transport constant. Even if the pore size of the electrode material is sufficient, ion diffusion frequently emerges as the limiting factor for overall charge transport. [ 120 ] It is important to highlight that there is often a lack of comparability among diffusion data acquired through different methods in the existing literature. [ 121 , 122 , 123 , 124 ] Even for systems with equivalent volume or pore space, variations in kinetic properties may arise due to diverse experimental approaches, and these differences can be accentuated under nanoconfinement. [ 125 ] Furthermore, steric hindrance related to diffusion can play a dual role. On one hand, it has the potential to modulate local reactant concentrations, thereby enhancing catalytic performance. On the other hand, it might obstruct active sites in nanoconfined spaces, leading to catalyst deactivation. Consequently, the diffusion behavior in nanoconfined spaces should be viewed dialectically. 2.2.2 Adsorption In the early stages, the assessment of adsorption under nanoconfinement focused on van der Waals interactions. Derouane et al. utilized a spherical pore model to compute the van der Waals attraction energy (W) for the guest molecule under various nanoconfined conditions (Equation ( 3 )). [ 126 , 127 ] (3) W = − C 4 d 3 1 − s 2 3 Here, C and d represent the molecular constant and adsorption distance, respectively. And s is the ratio of the adsorption distance to the radius of the spherical pore model. Specifically, s = 0 and s = 1 correspond to cases where the guest molecule is positioned in the plane and at the center of the spherical pore model, respectively. When the adsorption distance equals the radius of the pore, i.e., s = 1, the van der Waals attraction energy is eight times greater than the attraction energy on a flat surface ( s = 0). This observation underscores the significant impact of nanoconfinement on the physical adsorption of molecules. To directly assess the relationship between nanoconfinement and adsorption energy, the concept of confinement energy ( E con ) has been developed (Equation ( 4 )): (4) E c o n = E a d c o n − E a d u n c o n where E ad (con) and E ad (uncon) represent the adsorption energies with and without confinement, respectively. Taking CO adsorption on Pt(111) as an example, E ad changes from −1.94 eV for CO adsorption on the surface of Pt(111) to −1.50 eV for CO adsorption within Pt(111) and graphene cover. [ 128 ] The corresponding E con is 0.44 eV, suggesting that the graphene cover weakens CO adsorption on the surface of Pt(111). This finding contradicts the abovementioned results of nanoconfinement enhancing van der Waals adsorption. Although they are modeled differently—one as a spherical confinement space and the other as a 2D confinement space—this highlights the need to analyze nanoconfinement on a case‐by‐case basis. Similarly, Xiao et al. employed the E con to predict the impact of confinement on catalytic activity within carbon nanotubes. [ 129 ] They define the E con as the difference between the binding energy of an adsorbate molecule on a metal cluster confined to the inner wall of the carbon nanotube and that of a metal cluster located on the outer wall of the carbon nanotube (Equation ( 5 )): (5) E c o n = E b i n − E b o u t where E b (in) and E b (out) denote the binding energies of an adsorbate molecule on a metal cluster situated on the inner and outer walls of the carbon nanotube, respectively. When Fe, FeCo, RhMn, and Ru metal clusters are located on the inner wall, enhanced strain and deformation within the carbon nanotube channel occur due to distinct electronic structures and spatial confinement. Consequently, a decrease in the d‐band state results in weakened adsorption of molecules like CO, N 2 , and O 2 , as confirmed by positive confinement energies obtained. The consistent weakening of binding between adsorbate molecules with different intrinsic properties and metal clusters implies a general nanoconfinement effect on adsorption. However, varying binding energies for CO and N 2 with different metal clusters within the same type of carbon nanotube suggests that the nanoconfinement effect is metal‐specific. Additionally, by investigating electronic interactions between the catalyst and carbon nanotubes, E con was found to be highly correlated with the catalyst size, carbon nanotube diameter, and adsorbate coverage. For a given catalyst, E con increases with decreasing carbon nanotube diameter, and for a given carbon nanotube, E con increases with increasing catalyst size. [ 130 ] The observed positive E con is attributed to the heightened chemical potential of adsorbates in the confined space. Due to less perturbation of the confined environment, electronic interactions are less intense, destabilizing the potential surface formed between the adsorbate and the catalyst surface, resulting in a positive E con . This tunability of the chemical potential offers a promising approach to achieving exceptional activity and selectivity in catalytic reactions. [ 131 ] The adsorption of hydrogen, ethylene, and benzene on Fe, Ni, and Cu metal crystals with varying c ‐axis lengths offers a visual illustration of how nanoconfinement influences adsorption at a spatial scale. [ 132 ] The adsorption energy curves for these molecules exhibit analogous trends in response to variations in the length of the c ‐axis of the metal crystals, delineated into two regions of attraction and repulsion that influence the adsorption energy ( Figure 6 ). The cumulative effects of attractive and repulsive forces determine whether nanoconfinement has a positive or negative impact on the adsorption energy. Each curve exhibits an optimal space size that maximizes adsorption energy. Within this space, molecules can be activated for further transformation or highly adsorbed. For instance, single‐molecule microscopy studies have revealed that the confinement effect contributes to the formation and stabilization of carbon ions in zeolites. [ 133 , 134 ] The adsorption energy demonstrates a potential behavior along the c ‐axis, which can be modeled using the Lennard‐Jones (Equation ( 6 )) and Morse (Equation ( 7 )) potentials. (6) E = 4 ε σ c 12 − σ c 6 (7) E = ε e x p − 2 α c − c 0 − 2 e x p − α c − c 0 Figure 6 A model illustrating small molecules (hydrogen, ethylene, and benzene) confined to a surface oriented perpendicular to the c ‐axis of a metal crystal, along with their adsorption energy plotted against the length of the c ‐axis. Reproduced with permission. [ 132 ] Copyright 2019, Springer Nature. The parameters and variables in the equations are depicted schematically in Figure 6 . ɛ is a parameter common to both potentials, representing the depth of the potential well and interpreted as the bonding energy. The c 0 parameter in the Morse potential is the distance at which the minimum energy of inter‐particle separation occurs, while the σ parameter is the distance at which the potential energy is zero. For c ‐axis lengths below σ , the contribution of nanoconfinement to potential energy is dominated by repulsive forces, hindering adsorption and exerting a negative impact. When the c ‐axis length significantly exceeds σ , indicating a very large confinement space, the influence of confinement on the adsorption energy is minimal. Furthermore, nanoconfined metals tend to alter their electronic structure to achieve nearly the same density of states as in open space. That is, the instability introduced by nanoconfinement in the system may be counteracted by changes in electronic structure, facilitating the adsorption process. This phenomenon bears a resemblance to Le Chatelier's principle. In exploring adsorption within nanoconfined spaces, considering energy alone is insufficient; intermolecular interactions and coordination also exert significant influence on adsorption behavior. For instance, within nanoconfined spaces, most hydrogen bonds in the confined water adopt distorted tetrahedral structures or form broken hydrogen bonding networks, resulting in the reduction of some bonds to counterbalance the increase in chemical potential. Consequently, this enhances interactions of hydrogen bonds with certain adsorbate molecules, thus promoting adsorption. [ 135 ] Coordination effects in nanoconfined spaces primarily manifest in the coordination between adsorbates and the inner wall of the nanoconfined space, coordination between adsorbates and the surrounding solvent molecules, and coordination between adsorbates themselves. First, nanoconfined spaces induce spatial distortion in the coordination between the adsorbate and the surface of the confined space, consequently enhancing adsorption. [ 136 ] Second, in cases where adsorbates coordinate with surrounding water molecules, if the diameter of nanoconfined space is smaller than the hydration diameter of adsorbate ions, dehydration of adsorbate ions may occur. Subsequently, strong inner‐sphere coordination forms, boosting adsorption. This phenomenon is explained by the nanopore inner sphere enhancement effect, which necessitates the diameter of the nanopore inner sphere to be larger than the adsorbate ion but much smaller than the hydration diameter of the adsorbate ion. [ 137 , 138 ] Additionally, the cavity size of the nanopore inner sphere should not exceed about 0.3 to 0.5 nm in at least one dimension. Finally, nanoconfinement influences the coordination between adjacent adsorbates, thereby enhancing adsorption. For instance, interactions among arsenite adsorbates within nanoconfined spaces contribute to the improved adsorption capacity. [ 139 ] Adsorption behavior in nanoconfined spaces is also influenced by the previously mentioned nanoconfinement entropic effect. The adsorption isotherms reveal that the coverage of the nanoconfined system consistently surpasses the Langmuir isotherm of the macroscopic system. Consequently, the apparent adsorption constants of the nanoconfined system markedly exceed the Langmuirian value and increase as pressure and system size decrease. [ 140 ] The apparent adsorption constant, denoted as K n , is defined by Equation ( 8 ): (8) K n = θ n 1 − θ n p n where n signifies the equilibrium adsorption state where n molecules are adsorbed at n sites within a nanoconfined stoichiometric system. θ n represents the average coverage, and p n stands for the average pressure. The intensified adsorption in this nanoconfined system is linked to pressure fluctuations and the reduction in the entropy of mixing. Specifically, when considering this entropy effect in isolation, gas storage capacity is anticipated to be highest in very small pores, where one adsorption site is filled by one molecule (assuming the vanishing thickness of the wall). Additionally, simulations involving the competitive adsorption of two gases suggest that nanoconfined systems significantly enhance the selective adsorption of one of the gases. This finding holds potential significance for applications such as gas separation and selective catalysis in energy conversion processes. 2.2.3 Activation and Reaction The nanoconfined space imposes unique interactions on reactants, transition states, and products, modifying the reaction's overall energy profile. Compared to reactions in the bulk phase, nanoconfined reactions involve additional stages due to the encapsulation of reactants, the reactions occurring within the confinement, and the extraction of products. Each of these steps introduces specific energy barriers and changes in enthalpy, making the prediction of potential energy in nanoconfined reactions exceedingly complex. Notably, reactions under nanoconfinement can circumvent the high‐energy barrier to product formation in open space by leveraging these low‐energy stages, thereby favoring product formation. [ 141 ] In the hypothetical reaction where reactants A and B combine to form C, the energy barriers of each phase are reduced compared to the energy barrier in the bulk phase ( Figure 7 a ). For instance, the activation energy for water formation under confinement is merely half of that observed in the absence of confinement. [ 142 ] However, the overall kinetics of the nanoconfined reaction hinge on the cumulative effect of each step, encompassing the energy barrier of the rate‐determining step and any diffusion limitations. That is, even if the activation energy of the nanoconfined reaction is lower than that of the bulk‐phase reaction, the observed kinetics of the nanoconfined reaction might still experience significant delays if the steps involving reactant encapsulation or product extraction proceed sluggishly. [ 39 ] Thus, the influence of nanoconfinement on the reaction proves to be complex, often contingent on a multitude of factors. Figure 7 Simplified reaction profiles of a) A and B reacting to form C and b) A and B reacting to generate D and E under bulk environment and nanoconfinement. Reproduced with permission. [ 39 ] Copyright 2008, Royal Society of Chemistry. Moreover, nanoconfinement can bestow selectivity upon chemical reactions. In bulk environments, some reactions may show non or low selectivity. However, when the energy of a transition state is stabilized within the nanoconfined space, the energy barriers for the formation of multiple products significantly vary, resulting in high selectivity for specific products. [ 39 ] To illustrate, considering the production of products D and E from reactants A and B, specific interactions between the nanoconfined space and the encapsulated substrate may exert varying stabilizing effects on the transition states of D and E (Figure 7b ). Consequently, the reaction would favor the formation of E over product D due to the unstable transition state of D and the stabilized transition state of E. The selectivity governed by nanoconfinement is intricately linked to the interaction dynamics between the encapsulated substance and the nanoconfined space. In summary, nanoconfinement alters the thermodynamics and kinetics of reactions, offering certain advantages but also presenting potential disadvantages that must be considered. Table 1 outlines both the potential pros and cons of nanoconfinement. Balancing these trade‐offs between advantages and disadvantages is a crucial consideration when designing nanoconfined catalytic systems. Table 1 Summary of the potential pros and cons of nanoconfinement. Pros Cons Boosting reaction rates by increasing the collisions between reactants and active sites Nanoconfined spaces slow the diffusion rates of reactants entering and products exiting. Favoring chemical shifts by increasing local concentrations of reactants or intermediates. Oversized secondary structures may obstruct the entry and diffusion of molecules. Lowering activation energy barriers by adjusting the transition state The multiple phases of nanoconfined reactions make it challenging to monitor and interpret reaction kinetics. Enabling higher‐order reactions, such as carbon‐carbon coupling, by stabilizing intermediates Large products may block the nanoconfined space, reducing turnover rates and hindering product extraction and separation. Improving selectivity by screening reaction molecules through steric effects Tailoring selectivity by adjusting transition state barriers Enhancing stability by shielding active centers from agglomeration and harsh conditions John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.
title: Nanoconfinement Effects in Electrocatalysis and Photocatalysis.

text: 2 Materials and Methods 2.1 Materials Silver acetate (99.0%), silver nitrate (99.0%), amino-benzimidazole (≥95.0%), and ethanol (>99%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and used for surface modification. TFC RO membranes were supplied by GreEnvi Corp. (Canada). Sodium chloride (NaCl, 99.5%, Sigma-Aldrich) was utilized to prepare the feed solution. Bovine serum albumin (BSA), from Sigma-Aldrich, served as a model organic foulant. Luria–Bertani (LB) broth (Sigma-Aldrich) was used for the bacterial cell culture. (BL21­(DE3)) was used as a Gram-negative bacterium. Propidium iodide (PI) and SYTO9 (Molecular Probes) were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific. All chemicals were of analytical grade and used without further purification. 2.2 Synthesis of Ag-MAFs Two types of Ag-MAFs were synthesized for this study: one derived from the nitrate salt and the other from the acetate salt. An identical procedure was employed for both cases. For nitrate-based MAFs, 0.15 g of silver nitrate (AgNO 3 ) was dissolved in 30 mL of deionized water. Then, 0.1 g of amino-benzimidazole was dissolved in 25 mL of ethanol. Before synthesis, both solutions were thoroughly stirred and sonicated to achieve a homogeneous solution without agglomeration. The organic solution was added to the silver salt solution while stirring to induce precipitation. The mixture was stirred for 20 min to complete the reaction. Then, the precipitate was filtered and washed twice with 50 mL of fresh ethanol to remove any unreacted reagents. The same procedure was followed for synthesizing the acetate-based MAFs with different quantities of silver salt (0.12 g). 2.3 Surface Modification of TFC Membrane The polyamide TFC RO membranes were prepared via an interfacial polymerization (IP) process between MPD and TMC on the surface of the poly­(ether sulfone) (PES) substrate. The polyamide TFC membrane was fabricated by soaking the PES substrate in an aqueous solution containing 2 wt % MPD, 2 wt % CSA, 1 wt % TEA, and some additives for 2 min. The excess MPD solution was then carefully discarded from the membrane surface with a roller. The MPD-saturated membrane was immersed in a 0.1 wt/v % TMC solution containing n -hexane and an additive for 30 s to allow polyamide layer formation. Subsequently, the membrane was subjected to an oven at 80 °C for 5 min for post-thermal treatment. The IP reaction, based on the Schotten–Baumann mechanism, tends to be rapid and unregulated, leading to a nonuniform cross-linked polyamide active layer. The thermal treatment applied post-IP primarily serves to enhance polymer chain cross-linking, remove residual solvents, and improve membrane structural integrity, rather than driving the initial polymerization itself. Ag-MAFs were insitu deposited on the TFC membrane surface through a rapid and environmentally friendly procedure at room temperature. The residual acyl chloride functional groups present on the surface of the fresh TFC membrane undergo hydrolysis, transforming into carboxyl groups. , The RO membranes have many carboxylic groups spread over the polyamide surface. These carboxyl groups, carrying a negative charge, serve as active deposition sites for further modification. The strong interaction between the negatively charged moieties of the polyamide surface and the positively charged Ag ions leads to the adhesion of Ag particles to the membrane surface. Once the Ag ions are anchored to these sites, the amino-benzimidazole linker coordinates with the Ag atoms through a robust chemical interaction between the Ag ions and the amino-benzimidazole ligand. This interaction facilitates the formation of Ag-MAFs on the Ag-anchored sites, creating a functionalized membrane surface. The membrane surface was treated with silver salt, followed by ligand solutions to attach Ag-MAFs covalently.
